set.st: A land speculator 'who bore gold about his person' was found dead beneath his shattered window at the tavern, and the murderer was never found. Some months after the crime, a place beneath one of the giant oaks around the tavern was found where men had been digging in the night, presumably for gold buried there (Detroit News, 25 Jun 1922). The oak-digging story is in print by 1922; the 'money belt' detail appears only in the 1940s (WPA guide and later). Nine Potawatomi graves are said to lie under the big oak. Pin is the tavern crossroads, not a spot.
set.t: State historic site with graves under the oak: no digging, look only. The legend grows: 1919 a vanished guest and a 'murder room'; 1922 the reopening, a 'gold-laden traveler murdered' and a blood stain shown on tours, and the oak-digging story in the Detroit News; the 1940s add the money belt (repeated in a 1951 Detroit News Q&A, which has him found 'beneath the shattered window, in a crumpled heap on a flower bed'). No telling has a recovery, and the 1879 and 1909 county histories mention no murder.

src: Detroit News, 25 Jun 1922, p. 56, L. Y. Erskine, "A Landmark Restored" (Newspapers.com 1378667742)
